title: A small ending
hookLine: each sunset is a small ending

cards: Late afternoon light goes gold, then orange, then thin. The shadows stretch across the parking lot. Somebody on a beach claps when the last edge of the sun slips under the water, and nobody can quite say why.
A day is ending, the way days always do, and for a few minutes people stop to watch it end. This block of the path is about death, and the largest ending can only be imagined.
A smaller one comes around every evening, and it can be watched.

teach.h: THE SUN GOES DOWN AND HASTES.
teach.b: First, the sun goes down and hastes. Ecclesiastes watches the sky and sees a loop: "The sun also ariseth, and the sun goeth down, and hasteth to his place where he arose." The writer sounds a little weary of it.
But read another way, the line holds a quiet comfort: every ending in it is also on its way to a return.
Second, evening comes first. In Genesis, the days of creation close with a refrain: "And the evening and the morning were the first day." Evening is named before morning.
Jewish tradition reads this as one reason the day, and so Shabbat, begins at sundown. In this way of counting, the ending of the light is where a new day starts.

teach.h: A PRAYER AT THE SETTING SUN.
teach.b: Third, a prayer at the setting of the sun. In Islam, Maghrib, the sunset prayer, is prayed just after the sun goes down, so the end of each day is marked by stopping and turning toward prayer.
Other paths keep evening prayers too: some Christians pray vespers or compline, and Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at dusk.
A sunset is an ending you can practice on. It's safe, it's beautiful, and it always finishes.
Watching one all the way through, without looking away to your phone, trains something small: letting a thing be over, and finding that the world is still there afterward.

how: Muslims pray Maghrib just after sunset; Jews begin Shabbat and holy days at sundown; some Christians pray vespers or compline in the evening, and Sikhs recite Rehras Sahib at dusk.

practice: If the sun is setting where you are, watch it from a window; if not, choose another small ending you can see through, the last of a breath going out, a candle blown out, the final note of a song.

Watch it to the very end without hurrying or looking away, and when it's over, stay a moment in the quiet and notice what's still here. If you pray, an evening prayer from your own tradition fits this moment.

wordCard.voice: Maghrib, the Muslim sunset prayer that marks the day's end, like the sun in Ecclesiastes that hastens back to where it rose. Today's word.

orig.note: Hebrew: evening. in Genesis it's named first, and it's also the word for the eve of a holy day.
